prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect, and the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from B041 to B048. Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators introduced a genuinely new classification of band insulators, with the Z2 invariant, protected edge and surface states and a decisive HgTe transport experiment. The idea has spread to photonic, mechanical and cold-atom systems and has been confirmed independently for about two decades, so it is mature rather than premature. It is also the candidate with the broadest and most robust support across the committee: six members rank it, five of them in the top three, and two put it first. My own first choice, the hexatic melting work (B041), is scientifically a cornerstone of statistical mechanics, but only I ranked it, and I should not equate my own enthusiasm with committee-level merit.
statement.case_against: The credited set omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal sits between the Kane-Mele theory and the Molenkamp experiment, and also the three-dimensional topological insulator work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and of Hasan and Cava. The Kane-Mele graphene model is not the material realisation because the spin-orbit gap in graphene is tiny, so a citation must be worded carefully. The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter also partly overlaps in concepts. If the committee judges the attribution unresolvable within three names, B016 is the cleaner theory-plus-experiment triple.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B048 first as a clean pairing of the Z2 theory with the decisive HgTe experiment, mature and arguably overdue, while noting that the BHZ step and the 3D work sit just outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the weight of the evidence, and I have moved to B048 partly for that reason. I would qualify the word clean. The BHZ proposal is the specific hinge that made the HgTe experiment happen, so the citation should be phrased around the Z2 prediction and the experimental observation in HgTe rather than implying the whole chain is credited. Your remark about the graphene gap is also important, because it means the prediction was for a model and the material success came elsewhere.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B048 third and worries that the 2016 prize on topological phases and the omission of Zhang-type contributions weaken its priority, and she prefers the precision-measurement candidates B049 and B020 at the top.
responses.response: I take the 2016 overlap seriously, but I think it is smaller than it looks. The 2016 prize rewarded Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz for topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall topology of broken time-reversal symmetry. Time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators are a distinct discovery with protected edge states that need no magnetic field. That is why I put B048 above my own B041 (hexatic melting), which does sit closer to the Kosterlitz-Thouless foundations. On B049 I do not dispute the physics, but with only four members ranking it and a clean two-name credit it seems to me less broadly supported than B048, and the prior prizes for combs and ion clocks already cover much of the neighbouring ground.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks DMFT (B006) first as the standard non-perturbative framework for correlated electrons, mature and widely used, but notes that Metzner and the DFT+DMFT developers are not in the credit.
responses.response: I ranked B006 fourth and share the view that DMFT is an important statistical-physics idea. My reservation is attribution rather than merit. The infinite-dimension limit (Metzner and Vollhardt), the impurity mapping (Georges and Kotliar) and the early numerical solutions (Jarrell, Rozenberg and others) do not map cleanly onto three people, and the case rests on method more than on a discovery. Only two members rank it, so I would keep it as an option but not as the centre of a configuration.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B038) first as the architecture behind superconducting processors, and is candid about his own proximity to the field and about the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure. The importance of circuit QED is clear to me, but I find the timing and credit difficult. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits is close in subject, and four people (Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf, Wallraff) have a strong claim for three seats, as Lindroth and Olsson also note. Your own ballot rates topological insulators second, which suggests B048 could be a point of agreement between us.

uncertainties: Whether the attribution problem around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological insulator discoverers can be handled in a citation limited to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
How much weight the committee should give to the partial conceptual overlap with the 2016 prize.
Whether B016 (twisted bilayer graphene) is too early given the unsettled superconducting mechanism, or is the stronger choice because its theory-plus-experiment attribution is cleaner.
I am recalling the details of attribution for B041, B048 and B006 from memory and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no documented connection to any of the credited candidates in B048, B016 or B041. My neighbouring statistical-physics interest in topological defects and in B041 should be read as scientific interest, not a conflict.
